newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Ramos reaffirms commitment to one six-year term.
newsitem.headline: Ramos reaffirms commitment to one six-year term.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos on Wednesday reaffirmed his commitment to stepping down from office next year although he would not interfere with moves by legislators to extend the terms of elected officials.

"I am not interfering with the work of the house," Ramos said at his weekly news conference when asked about a resolution placed before the House of Representatives seeking to extend the terms of elected officials, including Ramos, until 2001.
Under the constitution, Ramos is limited to a single six-year term in office which ends in mid-1998. The terms of other officials are also limited, but to varying degrees.
Asked if he would step down next year, Ramos said: "I have made my position very clear. You please be the judge on whether I have delivered on my commitments."
Ramos said on Saturday that he did not support either extension of his term or any amendment of the constitution to enable him to seek re-election.
Earlier on Wednesday, Ramos signed the 1997 budget into law but vetoed a provision which sought to restrict the use of funds to underwrite any election or plebiscite this year.
The presidential palace said in a statement that Ramos used his veto powers because the provision impinged on the "fundamental prerogatives" of the Commission of Elections.
Opposition politicans have said the use of the veto suggests that the government may be considering a plebiscite to amend the constitution, possibly to extend Ramos's term.
"The possibility of holding a plebiscite to amend the constitution is now very distinct," opposition Senator Ernesto Herrera said.
"There is now a source of funding for this activity," he told reporters.
Ramos has however said that any amendment to the constitution will centre on protecting the government's economic reforms programme from litigation.

He made the comments last week after the Supreme Court struck down the sale of the historic Manila Hotel to a Malaysian company and awarded the property to a local firm in keeping with a "Filipino First policy".
Ramos said the judgment had struck a blow at the country's privatisation programme, the cornerstone of its reforms.
